scope.start: 16b: the Mishnah's *he'emid* clause and the dispute of Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda over a gentile's *tzon barzel* flock (opens mid-sugya)
scope.end: 18a: the reading of the *eglah arufah* baraita as a dispute over "*kerova*" (continues on 18a)

sections.title: Tzon Barzel Flock: One Generation Exempt or Two?
sections.gist: Continuing the Mishnah on a Jew who holds a gentile's flock as *tzon barzel*: Rav Huna exempts one generation of offspring and Rav Yehuda two. Their views are tested against the *he'emid* clause, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's "even ten generations", and the Mishnah's plain wording.

children.title: Without He'emid: Rav Huna (Offspring) vs. Rav Yehuda (Grandoffspring Too)
children.gist: Where the Jew did not set the offspring in place of their mothers, Rav Huna exempts only the direct offspring, and Rav Yehuda exempts their offspring as well.

bullets.text: The Mishnah: if the Jew set the offspring in place of their mothers (*he'emid*), as security in case the mothers die, the offspring's offspring are exempt from *bekhor*.

Rashi: *he'emid* means the Jew told the gentile he may collect from the offspring. Tosafot: the mothers died and the offspring took their place. Either way the gentile's claim moves down a generation.

In an ordinary *tzon barzel* arrangement, without *he'emid*: Rav Huna says the direct offspring are exempt and their offspring obligated. Rav Yehuda says their offspring are exempt too, and only the third generation is obligated.
The exemption rests on the gentile's right to seize: whichever generation he can collect from is exempt. Rav Yehuda sees that right reaching one generation further than Rav Huna does.

children.title: The He'emid Clause: A Contrast or a Ceiling?
children.gist: The Mishnah seems to exempt the grandoffspring only because of *he'emid*, refuting Rav Yehuda. He answers that the clause caps *he'emid* at two generations.

bullets.text: Objection: the Mishnah exempts the offspring's offspring *because* he set them in place of their mothers. That implies that without *he'emid* they are not exempt, a conclusive refutation of Rav Yehuda.
Rav Yehuda: the grandoffspring are exempt even without *he'emid*. The Mishnah teaches that even with *he'emid* only the first two generations are exempt, not every later generation.
The point is needed: one might think a gentile normally seizes young of any generation, so that with *he'emid* all generations would be exempt. The Mishnah says he is like one who did not *he'emid*.
On this reading the clause does not contrast *he'emid* with the ordinary case. It sets a limit on *he'emid* itself. It is a strained reading of the Mishnah.

children.title: "Even Ten Generations": What Is Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel Arguing Against?
children.gist: "Even" implies the first *tanna* also counted generations. That fits Rav Yehuda; Rav Huna answers that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel is addressing the *he'emid* case.

bullets.text: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: even until ten generations are exempt, since the gentile will collect from any offspring born to the animal or to its offspring.

"Even" implies that he disputes only how many generations are exempt, and agrees that some are. For Rav Yehuda this works: the first *tanna* went down two generations, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says even ten.

For Rav Huna, the first *tanna* counted no generations at all, so what does "even ten" mean? Answer: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel refers to the *he'emid* case, where the first *tanna* does go down a generation.
Once generations are being counted, several limits are possible, so Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel must state that there is no practical limit.

children.title: The Mishnah's Wording: "Offspring Exempt" or "They and Their Offspring"
children.gist: Two versions of the Mishnah's wording. Each version challenges one of the amora'im, and each amora rereads the words to fit his view.

bullets.text: The Mishnah: one who accepts animals as *tzon barzel* from a gentile: the offspring are exempt, and the offspring's offspring are not. This looks like a refutation of Rav Yehuda.
Rav Yehuda: read it as "they and their offspring are exempt". The "offspring" meant are the offspring of the direct offspring.
Another version: the Mishnah itself reads "they and their offspring are exempt", which looks like a refutation of Rav Huna.
Rav Huna: "they" are the original animals and "their offspring" the direct offspring. The offspring's offspring are obligated.
The dispute is not decided. Rav Huna's is the plainer reading of the Mishnah.

sections.title: R. Meir Obligates a Nidmeh: Firstborn, Shearing, or Oto Ve'et Beno?
sections.gist: A baraita has R. Meir obligating a sheep-like offspring of a goat. The Gemara rules out *bekhor* and the first shearing, tries paternity for *oto ve'et beno* and drops it, then reads the case as a lineage question, and finally takes Rav Ashi's reading of partial resemblance.

Ewe born to a goat born to a ewe

children.title: Nidmeh in the Mishnah vs. Rav Oshaya's Baraita
children.gist: The Mishnah exempts a *nidmeh* from *bekhor*, but the baraita has R. Meir obligating it.

bullets.text: The Mishnah: a ewe that gave birth to a goat of sorts, or a goat that gave birth to a ewe of sorts (a *nidmeh*), is exempt from *bekhor*.
Rav Oshaya came from Neharde'a with a baraita: an animal that looks like a ewe and was born to a goat, or a goat born to a ewe, is obligated according to R. Meir and exempt according to the Rabbis.
R. Meir seems to contradict the Mishnah's exemption. That raises the question of which obligation he means.

children.title: Not Bekhor, Not Reishit Ha'gez
children.gist: Rav Hoshaya asks Rabba what R. Meir obligates. Each obvious option collides with a rule R. Meir accepts.

bullets.text: Rav Hoshaya to Rabba: ask Rav Huna, in what does R. Meir obligate it?
Not *bekhor*: R. Meir agrees that "But the firstborn of an ox" (Bamidbar 18:17) requires the mother to be an ox and its firstborn an ox, meaning the young must look like its mother.

Not *reishit ha'gez* (the first shearing given to the kohen): the school of R. Yishmael taught that lambs with tough fleece are exempt, from "warmed with the fleece of my sheep" (Iyov 31:20). The goat-like young of a ewe has tough fleece.

children.title: Rabba: Chosheshin Le'zera Ha'av for Oto Ve'et Beno, Rejected
children.gist: Rabba reads the dispute as whether the father's line counts for slaughtering a parent and its young on one day. The Gemara objects that the baraita would then have used Chananya's general dispute.

bullets.text: Rabba: the case is a ewe that bore a goat of sorts whose father was a goat. The dispute is *chosheshin le'zera ha'av*, whether the father's line counts, for *oto ve'et beno*.
R. Meir: the father counts, so one who slaughters the male goat and its goat-like young on one day is liable. The Rabbis: the father does not count.
*Chosheshin le'zera ha'av* is not doubt about who the father is. It asks whether the father's tie to the young carries any legal weight among animals.
Objection: then they should dispute paternity in general, as Chananya and the Rabbis do (Chullin 78b). Why state it in the unusual case of a ewe that bore a goat of sorts? The reading is dropped.

children.title: Back to Bekhor: Follow the Mother or the Grandmother? Does the Species Return?
children.gist: The dispute is about *bekhor* after all, in a three-generation line: either a ewe from a ewe from a goat, or a ewe from a goat from a ewe.

bullets.text: A ewe born to a ewe born to a goat: it looks like its mother but not its grandmother. R. Meir: follow its mother, so it is not a *nidmeh* and the firstborn law applies.
The Rabbis: follow its mother's mother. It doesn't look like her, so it is a *nidmeh* and exempt.

Alternatively, a ewe born to a goat born to a ewe. R. Meir: its ovine nature was restored to its origin, so the firstborn law applies. The Rabbis: it was not restored; whenever the young is unlike its mother, it is exempt.
Underneath is the question whether *nidmeh* is only a rule about resembling the immediate mother, or a status that attaches to a line and passes down.

children.title: Rav Ashi: Some of the Mother's Features — R. Meir vs. R. Shimon
children.gist: Rav Ashi reads the baraita as a dispute over how much resemblance to the mother the firstborn law needs.

bullets.text: Rav Ashi: the young has some of its mother's features. R. Meir's view is that of the Mishnah here, which applies the firstborn law in such a case.
The dissenting "Rabbis" are R. Shimon: the young has firstborn status only if its head and most of its body look like its mother.
On this reading the dispute is only the threshold of resemblance, with no question of lineage or paternity.

sections.title: Shelo Nishtanah: An Unchanged Line for Offerings, Wool and Wine
sections.gist: Even R. Meir requires an unbroken line for the New Moon goat. Then a series of amora'im apply "unchanged" to wool for *kilayim*, *tekhelet* and *nega'im*, and Rav Ashi to wine, which Ravina tests with flax.

children.title: R. Yochanan: The New Moon Goat, "As Since the Six Days of Creation"
children.gist: Although R. Meir counts a ewe from a goat from a ewe as a firstborn, he concedes that the New Moon goat must come from an unbroken line of goats.

bullets.text: On the second reading, R. Meir counts a ewe born to a goat born to a ewe as a firstborn, although it doesn't look like its mother.

R. Yochanan: R. Meir concedes that the New Moon goat must be the son of a female goat. "And one male goat for a sin offering" (Bamidbar 28:15): "one" means distinctively a goat, as it has been since the six days of Creation.
Rashi: the New Moon goat stands for the goats of the *musaf* offerings generally.

An ancestor that merely looked like another species, with no crossbreeding, is enough to taint the line. That suggests *nidmeh* is more than a cosmetic oddity: it disturbs the animal's species identity.

returns_to.note: Builds on the second case: a ewe born to a goat born to a ewe

children.title: Two Verses: Kilayim and Nidmeh, Distant Ancestry and Gift Offerings
children.gist: Vayikra 22:27 already excludes a *nidmeh* from the altar, but each verse adds what the other would leave out.

bullets.text: Challenge: "When a bull, or a sheep, or a goat, is brought forth" (Vayikra 22:27) already teaches this. "A bull, or a sheep" excludes *kilayim* (a crossbreed), and "or a goat" excludes a *nidmeh*.

Both are needed. From Vayikra alone one would say it applies only where the resemblance doesn't trace back to an earlier generation; where it does, the animal is fit. Bamidbar adds "as since the six days of Creation".
From Bamidbar alone one would limit it to an obligatory offering, the subject of that verse, and not a gift offering.

children.title: Wool That Has Not Changed: Kilayim, Tekhelet, Nega'im
children.gist: Three amora'im each say "everyone concedes": wool of a *nidmeh* is not wool for *kilayim*, *tekhelet* or *nega'im*, because the Torah pairs wool with linen, which has not changed.

bullets.text: R. Acha bar Yaakov: everyone concedes there is no flogging for *kilayim* when wearing its wool with linen. "Wool and linen together" (Devarim 22:11): just as linen has not changed, so the wool must come from an animal that has not changed.
Rav Pappa: everyone concedes its wool is unfit as the *tekhelet* of *tzitzit*, since "you shall make yourself twisted cords" (Devarim 22:12) follows the verse on wool and linen.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: everyone concedes its wool does not become impure with *nega'im*, from "a woolen garment, or a linen garment" (Vayikra 13:47).
"Everyone" includes R. Meir: whatever his view on the firstborn law, wool from a changed line is not wool in the legal sense.

children.title: Vine Trellised on a Fig: Wine Unfit for Libations; Ravina's Flax Challenge
children.gist: Rav Ashi extends "unchanged" to wine. Ravina objects that flax could be changed the same way, and Rav Ashi replies that scent is the test.

bullets.text: Rav Ashi: if one trellised a vine over a fig tree, its wine is unfit for libations. "An offering, and libations" (Vayikra 23:37): as the offering must be unchanged, so must the libation.
Ravina: then flax trellised over a shrub is changed too, and R. Acha bar Yaakov's "just as linen has not changed" fails.
Rav Ashi: the wine's scent has changed, but the flax's scent has not, so its alteration does not count.
Grapes take on the character of what they grow near, but flax stays fixed short of an actual crossbreed. So flax remains a sound benchmark for the whole series.

sections.title: Mishnah: Twin Firstborn Males — Both to the Kohen, or One Came First?
sections.gist: Two males whose heads emerged as one: R. Yosei HaGelili gives both to the kohen, and the Rabbis hold that births cannot coincide precisely. The Mishnah then rules on the doubtful twin, on a twin that died, and on a male and female born together.

It stays with the owner: the burden of proof rests on the claimant

children.title: Heads Emerging as One: Both to the Kohen, or Ein Efshar Le'tzamtzem
children.gist: R. Yosei HaGelili gives both twins to the kohen. The Rabbis say one must have come first, so one twin goes to the kohen, and R. Tarfon and R. Akiva dispute which one.

bullets.text: A ewe that had not given birth before bore two males, and both heads emerged as one. R. Yosei HaGelili: both go to the kohen, as it says in the plural, "the males shall be to the Lord" (Shemot 13:12).
The Rabbis: *ein efshar le'tzamtzem*, two events cannot coincide precisely. One preceded the other, so one goes to the owner and one to the kohen.
R. Tarfon: the kohen chooses the better of the two. R. Akiva: their value is assessed, and the kohen takes the leaner.
The owner may not eat his lamb, since it may be the firstborn. It grazes until it is blemished, and then he may slaughter and eat it.
R. Yosei HaGelili trusts births that appear simultaneous. The Rabbis assume an imperceptible priority that no one can identify.

children.title: The Doubtful Twin: Priestly Gifts, a Twin That Died, Male and Female
children.gist: The rest of the Mishnah: whether the owner's twin owes the priestly gifts, what happens if one twin died, and the case of a male and a female.

bullets.text: When the owner slaughters his twin, he must give the priestly gifts due from a non-sacred animal: the foreleg, the jaw and the maw. R. Yosei exempts him.
If one of the two died: R. Tarfon says the kohen and the owner divide the survivor. R. Akiva says it stays with the owner, since the burden of proof rests on the claimant.
If a male and a female were born together, everyone agrees the kohen gets nothing.

sections.title: Efshar Le'tzamtzem in Human Hands? Altar Line, Measurements, Oven, Eglah Arufah
sections.gist: The Rabbis deny precise coincidence in events in Heaven's hands; the Gemara asks about events in human hands. Four proofs (the altar's red line, the Temple measurements, a split oven, the *eglah arufah*) are each deflected, and a tannaitic dispute is reread as being about "nearest".

chart.caption: Proofs about precision in human hands, and how each is deflected
rows: Red line on the altar (Middot 3:1)
People can find the exact midpoint, or blood would be put on the wrong half
The line is widened a little, so it surely covers the middle
Measurements of the vessels and altar
The Torah's exact measurements assume precision is possible
"Do it": whatever one can achieve is accepted (I Divrei HaYamim 28:19)
Impure oven split in two (Rav Ketina)
Equal halves both stay impure, so precision is impossible
Rav Kahana: earthenware breaks unevenly and is hard to measure
*Eglah arufah* between two towns (Sota 45b)
R. Eliezer's two heifers assume precision is possible
R. Eliezer holds like R. Yosei HaGelili; this tells nothing of the Rabbis

children.title: School of R. Yannai: In Heaven's Hands vs. in Human Hands
children.gist: R. Yosei HaGelili allows precision in events in Heaven's hands, and all the more so in human hands. The Rabbis deny the first; their view on the second is the question.

bullets.text: School of R. Yannai: R. Yosei HaGelili holds *efshar le'tzamtzem* for events in Heaven's hands, and all the more so for events in human hands, which are meant to be simultaneous.
The Rabbis hold it impossible in Heaven's hands. What do they hold about events in human hands?
"In human hands" can mean that a person made the situation, or that a person could measure it. The proofs that follow point to the second: the chance to measure.

children.title: The Red Line on the Altar: Widened to Cover the Middle
children.gist: The altar's midline suggests people can find an exact middle. The answer is that the line is widened so it surely covers it.

bullets.text: Middot 3:1: a red line circled the altar at its middle, dividing blood placed above from blood placed below. If human precision were impossible, blood for the upper part would sometimes land below and vice versa.
Rejection: the line is widened a little, so that it certainly covers the middle.
This proves only that the system tolerates imprecision, not that precision is possible.

children.title: Measurements of the Vessels and Altar: "Do It" as Best You Can
children.gist: The Torah's exact dimensions for the Temple vessels don't prove that precision is possible: a best effort suffices where the Torah says "do it".

bullets.text: Proof: the Torah gives exact measurements for the vessels and the altar, so precise measurement must be possible.
Rejection: there the Merciful One said "do it", and whatever one can achieve finds favor. "All this in writing, as the Lord has made me wise by His hand upon me" (I Divrei HaYamim 28:19).
A best-effort standard like this could explain R. Yosei HaGelili generally, but the Gemara limits it to acts the Torah commands.

children.title: An Impure Oven Split in Two: Both Impure, or Just an Uneven Break?
children.gist: Rav Ketina brings a baraita that treats equal halves of an oven as impossible to measure; Rav Kahana answers that earthenware breaks unevenly.

bullets.text: Rav Ketina: an impure earthenware vessel is purified only by breaking. The larger piece stays impure and the smaller becomes pure. If an impure oven was split into two equal pieces, both are impure, since they cannot coincide precisely.
Rav Kahana: earthenware is different, because the break has indentations and is especially hard to measure.

children.title: Eglah Arufah Between Two Towns: R. Eliezer's Two Heifers
children.gist: R. Eliezer has two equidistant towns each bring a heifer, which assumes precise measurement is possible. The Gemara answers that he simply follows R. Yosei HaGelili.

bullets.text: Mishnah (Sota 45b): if the slain man was found precisely between two towns, both bring heifers. This is R. Eliezer's view.

The reason: he holds precision is possible in human hands, and reads "the town which is nearest" (Devarim 21:3) as including two equidistant towns. Otherwise they would bring one heifer in partnership, on condition that it belongs to the town actually nearer.
Rejection: R. Eliezer holds like R. Yosei HaGelili, that precision is possible in Heaven's hands and all the more so in human hands. He tells us nothing about the Rabbis.
No one placed the body there. The case counts as "in human hands" because the distance can be measured afterwards.

children.title: No Heifer or Two Heifers: Precision, or the Singular "Kerova"?
children.gist: A baraita's dispute over the equidistant corpse looks like a dispute about precision. The Gemara rereads it: everyone agrees precision is possible, and they disagree whether "nearest" can mean more than one town.

bullets.text: Baraita: if the slain man was found precisely between two towns, no heifer's neck is broken at all. R. Eliezer: the two towns bring two heifers. Is the first *tanna*'s view that precision is impossible?
Rejection: if the first *tanna* held precision impossible, he would have them bring one heifer in partnership, on condition that it is for the town actually nearer, rather than none.
Rather, all agree precision is possible. The first *tanna* reads the singular "*kerova*" as only one nearest town, not several. R. Eliezer holds that it includes several.

returns_to.note: Returns to R. Eliezer's two heifers, now in a baraita with a dissenting first tanna

key_terms.definition: An arrangement in which one party receives animals or other property to use and profit from, while guaranteeing their full value to the owner whatever happens to them.
key_terms.on_this_daf: A gentile's flock held by a Jew as *tzon barzel* is exempt from the firstborn law, and Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda dispute how many generations of offspring share the exemption.

key_terms.sense: firstborn male of a kosher domestic animal
key_terms.definition: The first male born to a cow, sheep or goat, which is holy from birth and given to a kohen. It is exempt if a gentile has a share in the mother.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The daf asks which offspring of a gentile's flock are exempt, whether an animal unlike its mother is a firstborn, and what happens with twin males.

key_terms.definition: An animal born to one species that looks like a different species, such as a sheep-like young born to a goat.
key_terms.on_this_daf: R. Meir and the Rabbis dispute whether resemblance is judged by the mother or by earlier generations, and several amora'im disqualify a *nidmeh* line for offerings, *tekhelet*, *kilayim* and *nega'im*.

key_terms.sense: legal weight of an animal's paternity
key_terms.definition: The question whether an animal's father counts as its parent in halakha, for instance for the prohibition of slaughtering a parent and its young on the same day.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rabba proposes it as the subject of R. Meir's dispute over a goat-like young whose father was a goat; the Gemara drops the proposal.

key_terms.sense: material that has not changed from its kind
key_terms.definition: The requirement, learned by pairing a material with linen or with an offering, that wool or wine come from a source whose nature has not been altered.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Wool from a *nidmeh* line does not count for *kilayim*, *tekhelet* or *nega'im*, and wine from a vine trellised on a fig is unfit for libations; flax counts as unchanged because its scent does not change.

key_terms.sense: exact coincidence of two events or measures
key_terms.definition: The question whether two events or quantities can be treated as exactly simultaneous or exactly equal, or whether one must be assumed to precede or exceed the other.
key_terms.on_this_daf: R. Yosei HaGelili holds precision possible even in Heaven's hands, so twins can both be firstborn. The Rabbis deny it there, and the Gemara tests their view on events in human hands.

key_terms.sense: heifer whose neck is broken for an unsolved killing
key_terms.definition: The heifer brought by the town nearest to a corpse found in open country when the killer is unknown; its neck is broken and the elders declare their innocence.
key_terms.on_this_daf: R. Eliezer has two equidistant towns bring two heifers, which the Gemara examines as evidence that precise measurement is possible.

judgment_calls: Rav Huna vs. Rav Yehuda (16b.9–17a.3) is split into four children following the Gemara's four moves (the dispute, the he'emid objection, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, the Mishnah's wording); a flatter single section was possible, but the alternating challenges to each amora are clearer as separate steps.

R. Yochanan on the New Moon goat (17a.13) opens on the second reading of the baraita and could sit inside the nidmeh-baraita section (s6); placed it as the opening of the 'unchanged line' section because it and its two-verse discussion introduce the series on unchanged wool and wine, with a returns_to link to s10.

Rav Ashi's partial-resemblance reading (s11) is kept as the last child of the baraita section, in text order, although it is an alternative to the whole line of readings rather than a further step in it.
The twins Mishnah is split into the main dispute (s18) and the rest of the Mishnah (s19), so the part the shiur doesn't cover can carry its own flag.

The baraita on the equidistant corpse (s26) shifts from precision to the reading of 'kerova'; kept under the precision section because it starts as another test of the same question, with a returns_to link to s25.
The chart of R. Tarfon vs. R. Akiva sits on the Mishnah parent (s17) because its second column comes from the part of the Mishnah in s19.
coverage_notes: Scope ends at 18a.5, but the provided text runs only through 18a.4. The last section is anchored to 18a.5, and nothing beyond 18a.4 is stated.

17b.1 (priestly gifts from the doubtful twin, a twin that died, male and female) and 18a.2–18a.4 (the baraita on the equidistant corpse and the 'kerova' reading) are not discussed in the shiur; outlined from the text only.
The essay describes R. Akiva as giving the kohen half the difference in value; the text says the value is assessed and the kohen takes the leaner. Followed the text.
The essay explains that the owner's twin grazes because it can't be offered (chullin in the Azarah); the text says he may not eat it because of its doubtful firstborn status. Followed the text.
The essay discusses Rav Ashi's partial-resemblance answer after the whole purity series; in the text it comes at 17a.12, before R. Yochanan. Followed the text's order.
The essay calls the source of 'one who accepts tzon barzel from a gentile: offspring exempt' a baraita; the text calls it the Mishnah. Followed the text.
The essay says the grapes' smell and taste changed; the text mentions only scent. It also attributes the reply to Ravina to 'the Gemara'; the text has Rav Ashi reply. Followed the text.
The essay speaks of a broken pottery vessel and attributes the rejection to 'the Gemara'; the text has Rav Ketina cite a baraita about an oven and Rav Kahana reject it. Followed the text.
The essay extends the tekhelet ruling to priestly garments; the text mentions only ritual fringes. Followed the text.
The essay says the Gemara notes that R. Meir and R. Shimon sometimes swap roles as anonymous majority and dissent; this is not in the text and was omitted.
The essay says the daf ends with the question unresolved after the eglah arufah proof; the text rejects that proof (18a.1) and goes on to the baraita and the 'kerova' reading. Followed the text.
The text has 'Rav Oshaya came from Neharde'a' and then 'Rav Hoshaya said to Rabba'; both spellings are kept as the text has them.
The essay describes R. Yochanan's requirement as for the communal musaf sin offering generally; the text speaks of the New Moon goat, with the Rashi note on musafim kept as shiur.
